newsitem.title: KENYA: Aid workers doubt wisdom of Zaire airdrop plan.
newsitem.headline: Aid workers doubt wisdom of Zaire airdrop plan.

text.p: Aid workers on Thursday poured scorn on a Canadian plan to airdrop food to thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire, saying the proposal was expensive, dangerous and full of holes.

The Zairean government added its weight to the dissenting voices when its information minister said the huge central African nation would not accept the plan floated by the Canadians and under consideration by the U.S.

Many said airdrops would require good intelligence on the whereabouts of the refugees -- until now a mystery -- and some presence on the ground to ensure that supplies reached refugees in need instead of Hutu militiamen or Zairean troops.

"This (airdrop plan) is a demonstration of the impotence and desperation of the international community," a Nairobi-based aid worker told Reuters. "How do you airdrop supplies when you have no clue as to the whereabouts of the people you are supposed to be helping?"
Canada, leading a planned U.N.-authorised military relief effort, has proposed parachuting food over Zaire from a base in neighbouring Uganda, which lacks good road links with east Zaire.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, visiting NATO's southern command in Naples, Italy, on Wednesday ruled out sending a U.S. combat force to Zaire but said Washington was ready to take part in the Canadian airdrop proposal.
Several countries have tentatively offered to take part in the military relief effort but have yet to decide the next step.
In recent years food supplies have been parachuted to Moslems in Bosnia and to Kurds in northern Iraq where some falling crates killed or injured civilians.

"In places like eastern Zaire where the refugee population is likely to be highly concentrated on one area, the business of airdropping supplies becomes very dangerous. The best you could do is find these people and return them home," another aid worker said.
Some said the most urgently needed supplies were water and this could not be airdropped to the refugees.
"One of the things the refugees need most is water and you certainly cannot airdrop this commodity," said an aid worker with airdropping experience in southern Sudan.

Brenda Barton, spokeswoman for the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) in Kenya, said the food agency would consider airdrops to the estimated 600,000 wandering refugees scattered in eastern Zaire only as a last resort.
"We only start airdrops when we have no other option. It is a last resort and an expensive one as well," Barton said.

Diplomats said the plan was also likely to run headlong into operational problems because the rebels are opposed to the idea of outside forces coming to the aid of the refugees -- with Hutu extremists in their midst -- inside Zaire.
With Rwanda's backing, the rag-tag rebel army is ready to veto authority for flights over its territory.
"This in itself kills the operation before it even takes off," an African diplomat said.
The return home of up to 600,000 Rwandan Hutus has weakened support for a planned multinational military force, vehemently opposed by Rwanda.

The Canadian commander of a proposed multinational force Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril met rebel leader Laurent Kabila in the rebel-held town of Goma on Thursday but no details were available at the end of their meeting.

"But it is highly unlikely that Kabila would go against Rwanda's wishes and agree to Baril's request. I would imagine that the general got nothing out of the rebels," an African ambassador told Reuters.
The Rwandan Hutu refugees fled to east Zaire in fear of reprisals for a 1994 Hutu-led genocide of minority Tutsis after which a Tutsi-dominated army swept to power in Rwanda.
